{{short description|Swiss mathematician and philosopher}}
[[File:Ferdinand Gonseth ETH-Bib Portr 00116.jpg|thumb|Ferdinand Gonseth]]
'''Ferdinand Gonseth''' (1890–1975) was a Swiss mathematician and philosopher.<ref name="CTHS">{{cite web|url=http://cths.fr/an/prosopo.php?id=117881|title=Gonseth, Ferdinand CTHS|accessdate=10 May 2017}}</ref>

He was born on 22 September 1890 at [[Sonvilier]], the son of Ferdinand Gonseth, a clockmaker, and his wife Marie Bourquin. He studied at [[La Chaux-de-Fonds]], and read physics and mathematics at [[ETH Zurich]], from 1910 to 1914.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.hls-dhs-dss.ch/textes/f/F31363.php|title=Gonseth, Ferdinand, Dictionnaire historique de la Suisse|accessdate=10 May 2017}}</ref>

In 1929 Gonseth succeeded [[Jérôme Franel]] as Professor of Higher Mathematics at ETH.<ref>{{cite book|author1=[[Günther Frei]]|author2=[[Urs Stammbach]]|title=Die Mathematiker an den Zürcher Hochschulen|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=f4n0BQAAQBAJ&pg=PA54|date=7 March 2013|publisher=Springer-Verlag|isbn=978-3-0348-8542-3|page=54|language=de}}</ref> In 1947 he founded ''[[Dialectica]]'', with [[Paul Bernays]] and [[Gaston Bachelard]]. In the same year he took the newly created chair of [[philosophy of science]] at ETH.<ref>{{cite book|author=Charles P. Enz|title=No Time to be Brief: A Scientific Biography of Wolfgang Pauli|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=LdMVAwAAQBAJ&pg=PA414|date=6 May 2010|publisher=OUP Oxford|isbn=978-0-19-958815-2|page=414}}</ref>

Gonseth died on 17 December 1975 at [[Lausanne]].<ref name="CTHS"/> He was noted for his "open philosophy", according to which science and mathematics lacked absolute foundations.<ref>{{cite book|author1=[[Solomon Feferman]]|chapter= Correspondence with Paul Bernays|title=Kurt Gödel: Collected Works: Volume IV: Selected Correspondence, A-G|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=vZjlAgAAQBAJ&pg=PA43|date=9 January 2014|publisher=Clarendon Press|isbn=978-0-19-100376-9|page=43}}</ref> See {{ill|Idoneism|fr|Idonéisme}}.
